**Extract:**

**Soapy Sudds Manufacturer (SSM)**

SSM is a public limited company that was set up 25 years ago. SSM manufacture soap powder in country Y. The soap powder is used for washing clothes. SSM sells all its soap powder to large retailers in country Y. SSM’s sales have been increasing for many years in country Y but sales in the last year have remained the same. The directors of SSM are considering ways to increase sales.

SSM has a total of 100 employees with 60 in the Operations Department. It uses flow production in the factory and has 10 production lines with 5 workers and 1 supervisor for each line. The Operations Manager is aware that production workers are unhappy and often complain about their jobs being boring. These workers have always been paid by an hourly rate. The Human Resources Manager has recommended changes to ensure fewer workers leave each year to work for other businesses.

The directors of SSM have decided to expand the factory. They will need \$15m to do this. The directors have also considered taking over a competitor. SSM is likely to benefit from economies of scale as it grows.

The Marketing Director thinks SSM should start selling soap powder in markets in other countries. SSM will need to carry out either primary market research or secondary market research to forecast the potential total sales in these new markets. There are many existing manufacturers in these countries. SSM need to consider the problems when entering new markets in other countries such as tariffs or quotas.

**Appendix 1**

**Manufacturing process to make soap powder**

All the different types of soap powder are manufactured on production lines using flow production. SSM makes use of specialisation.

Each production line has the following stages:

![Flowchart of soap powder production: Stage 1 - raw materials mixed; Stage 2 - released onto conveyor belt; Stage 3 - packaged; Stage 4 - quality checks; Stage 5 - stored.](assets/001-flowchart-of-soap-powder-production-stage-1-raw-.png)

Each of these stages uses machinery controlled by a production worker

Appendix 2

Email from the SSM Finance Director to the Managing Director

SSM has a cash-flow problem which may get worse. Please see charts below

![Two bar graphs comparing days taken to pay SSM (left) and SSM paying suppliers (right) from 2019 to 2021. Both graphs show increasing trends.](assets/002-two-bar-graphs-comparing-days-taken-to-pay-ssm-l.png)

**Appendix 3**

**Newspaper article from Main News 1 October 2021**

Retailers have reported increased sales for most types of products such as sales of washing machines which have increased by 15%. Economic growth in country Y is predicted to increase.

Many businesses have been recruiting additional employees and there are now shortages of some skilled workers. The government in country Y has recorded an increase in inflation to 8% so far this year, which is a worry.

Consider how SSM could benefit from the following three methods to achieve break even.

- Reducing variable costs
- Increasing selling price
- Reducing fixed costs

Which method is likely to have the greatest effect on SSM achieving break even? **Justify** your answer.

Refer to the following [insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2021-paper-2-case-study---new.pdf) when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
Reducing variable costs would help SSM achieve break even by lowering the cost per unit of soap powder produced. SSM could negotiate better prices for raw materials or improve production efficiency to reduce waste. This would decrease the variable cost per unit, meaning fewer units need to be sold to cover total costs and reach break even point. Given SSM's worsening cash flow position, reducing variable costs would directly improve profitability on each unit sold.

Increasing selling price would raise the contribution per unit, reducing the number of units SSM needs to sell to break even. However, in the competitive soap powder market, price increases risk losing customers to competitors. SSM would need to ensure any price rise doesn't significantly reduce demand, as this could actually move the business further from break even if sales volume falls too much.

Reducing fixed costs would lower SSM's break even point by decreasing the total costs that must be covered. This could involve reducing overheads like rent, salaries, or administrative expenses. However, with the planned £15 million factory expansion, SSM's fixed costs are likely to increase rather than decrease in the short term.

Reducing variable costs is likely to have the greatest effect on SSM achieving break even. As a manufacturer using flow production to make soap powder, variable costs represent a significant proportion of total costs. Small reductions in variable costs per unit multiply across SSM's large production volumes, creating substantial savings. Unlike price increases, cost reductions don't risk losing customers in the competitive market. While fixed cost reductions help, they're harder to achieve given SSM's expansion plans and may compromise long-term growth.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each method identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the method
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact on break even
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which method is most/least effective for achieving break even
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Reducing variable costs**
> 
>   - Negotiate better raw material prices or improve production efficiency → lower variable cost per unit
>   - Fewer units needed to be sold to cover total costs and reach break even point
>   - Directly improves profitability on each unit sold, helping SSM's worsening cash flow position
> 
> - **Increasing selling price**
> 
>   - Higher selling price → increased contribution per unit → fewer units needed to break even
>   - Risk of losing customers to competitors in the competitive soap powder market
>   - Potential reduction in sales volume could move business further from break even
> - **Reducing fixed costs**
> 
>   - Lower fixed costs → reduced total costs that must be covered → lower break even point
>   - Could involve cutting overheads like rent, salaries or administrative expenses
>   - Difficult to achieve given the planned £15 million factory expansion which will increase fixed costs
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - Reducing variable costs: gives the greatest effect because variable costs represent a significant proportion of total costs for a manufacturer using flow production, and small reductions multiply across large production volumes
>   - Increasing selling price: risky strategy that could lose customers in competitive market and potentially reduce sales volume
>   - Reducing fixed costs: harder to achieve given expansion plans and may compromise long-term growth, making this the least effective option

parts.problem_md: Do you think break-even analysis is always useful to managers in decision making? **Justify** your answer.
parts.solution_md:
On the positive side, break-even analysis provides clear financial targets **[K]** by showing exactly how many units need to be sold to cover costs, helping managers make informed pricing and production decisions **[An]**

It also simplifies complex financial information into easy-to-understand calculations **[K]** which enables quick comparisons between different business options and supports strategic planning **[An]**

However, break-even analysis assumes that costs and prices remain constant **[K]** which is unrealistic in dynamic markets, leading to inaccurate predictions and poor decision making **[An]**

It also ignores external factors like competitor actions and market conditions **[K]** which can significantly impact sales volumes, making the analysis less reliable for long-term planning **[An]**

Overall, break-even analysis is most useful for short-term operational decisions where variables are relatively stable **[E]**. However, for strategic long-term decisions involving market uncertainty, managers should combine break-even analysis with other tools like market research and scenario planning. This balanced approach ensures more comprehensive decision making **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - You are writing a mini-argument with a decision
> 
>   - Give one relevant reason to support your view → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this reason helps decision making (cause-effect chain) → 1 An mark
>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also impact decision making → 1 An mark
>   - Make a decision — which argument is stronger or more important overall? → up to 2 E marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Easy to calculate and understand [k] so saves time in decision making [an]
>   - Only considers financial factors [k] so may ignore qualitative aspects [an]
>   - Other appropriate responses should also be credited
> - Justification might include:
> 
>   - Break-even analysis assumes costs remain constant [k] which is unrealistic in volatile markets [an]. However, it provides clear targets [k] helping managers set realistic sales goals [an].
>   - Break-even analysis is not always useful as it oversimplifies complex business situations [eval].
>   - It works best for short-term decisions where variables are stable, but strategic decisions require additional analysis tools [eval]
> - The answer must focus on the usefulness of break-even analysis in decision making so do not accept general points about break-even analysis unless clearly linked to decision making

Customers order online from the FO website. The furniture is then delivered to customers in country Z using FO’s own delivery vehicles. However, FO is considering changing to selling its furniture through either wholesalers or large retailers in country Z.

The Chan family have the business objective of contributing to sustainable development. FO only uses sustainably sourced wood when making furniture. This is from local forests in country Z and the wood is more expensive than imported alternatives.

FO need to manage all its resources effectively. It tries to use the same components such as nails, brackets and paint for all its furniture designs. It is important to not run out of raw materials and so orders to suppliers must be carefully planned to avoid late deliveries. FO want to keep wastage of materials to a minimum. FO also need to consider how many employees are required to complete each order.
